name: Khiyâlî
bio: Khiyali was a native of Asia Minor who came to Constantinople, according to Gibb's Biographical Notices.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poems.title: One with Realms Eternal This My Soul
poems.author: Khiyâlî
poems.text:
One with Realms Eternal this my soul to make; what wouldest say?
All Creation's empire's fancies to forsake; what wouldest say?

Wearing to a hair my frame with bitter sighs and moans, in love,
Nestling in the Fair One's tresses, rest to take; what wouldest say?

Yonder gold-faced birds within the quicksilver-resplendent deep:
Launching forth the hawk, my striving, these to take; what wouldest say?

Yonder Nine Smaragdine Bowls of Heaven to quaff at one deep draught,
Yet from all ebriety's fumes free to break; what wouldest say?

To an autumn leaf the Sphere hath turned Khiyâlî's countenance;
To the Spring of Beauty, that a gift to make; what wouldest say?

poems.title: A Mejnun I, filled with the grace of Leyla
poems.author: Khiyâlî
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (1904)
poems.text:
A Mejnun I, filled with the grace of Leyla;
Within my head the passion-craze of Leyla.

That butt am I of Fate and evil Fortune
Who drowneth in the ocean-maze of Leyla.

To me Love's gory-shrouded martyr seemeth
Each tulip in the desert-ways of Leyla.

The Mejnun heart doth feel but shame at honour
Since branded with the dear disgrace of Leyla.

A silent Mejnun I, fulfilled of rapture,
But in my heart the deaf'ning praise of Leyla.

There falleth on mine ear the anklet's tinkle;
Will e'er appear or glimpse or trace of Leyla?

Till with the inner eye thou see'st, Khayali,
Ne'er will appear the lovely face of Leyla.

poems.title: My verses form the burden sung by all the feres of pain and pine
poems.author: Khiyâlî
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (1904)
poems.text:
My verses form the burden sung by all the feres of pain and pine;
A story from the world of Love is every single word of mine.

To laud the idols in the convent of the world my sighs and tears
Do furnish, these the organ notes, and those the ruby-tinted wine.

Although the Erzheng is no longer, every verse of mine doth glow
The picture-gallery of Mani, through the tale of thee divine.

Betake thee to the tomb of Mejnun and behold how Leyla makes
Of every bow of him a surma-holder for her painted eyne.

Behold, Khayali, thou'rt the champion-wrestler in the field of verse
To-day while reigneth a Darius heaven-throned and Jem-benign.

poems.title: Each tree within the mead I held a houri lighted here below
poems.author: Khiyâlî
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (1904)

poems.title: Naught he knows of medicine's virtue who hath ne'er had ache or pain
poems.author: Khiyâlî
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (1904)
poems.text:
Naught he knows of medicine's virtue who hath ne'er had ache or pain;
Never doth the caitiff quaff the beaker at the feast of bane.

He shall not be broiled at fires infernal myriad months and years,
He, O zealot, who in cant's hot market-place doth cold remain.

What though I should dance around, O jurist, for the Dear One's love? --
'Twere but meet if dust to circle with the whirlwind still be fain.

One of pinion with the Anqa lofty-souled is he to-day
Who apart, alone, abideth mid creation's nest and grain.

Tidings of the bloom and perfume of this garth Khayali gives,
Like to yonder leaf autumnal on whose green's the yellow stain.

poems.title: The world-adorners in the world know naught of what adornments be
poems.author: Khiyâlî
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (1904)

poems.title: Once unto the world-illuming Sun the Moon in heaven did say
poems.author: Khiyâlî
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (1904)
poems.text:
Once unto the world-illuming Sun the Moon in heaven did say,
'O thou beauty, radiance-visaged, charmer high of fair array,

''Tis thy beaker's dregs that scatter foison over land and sea,
'Whelmed are all earth's myriad atoms in the lustre of thy ray;

'Through thy self the verdant garden finds its glory and its grace,
'By the brilliance of thy judgment heaven and earth are lumined aye.

'What the sin whereof I'm guilty, what my evil in thy sight,
'That whene'er I look upon thee, thou dost turn thy face away?

'That whene'er I show to thee my body bended as the bow
'Far thou fliest to the apsis of disdain and there dost stay?'

When these words the Moon had spoken reached unto the shining Sun,
Thus the answer came, 'O mirror of the forms of man and fay,

'Whensoe'er thou art beholden in the fulness of thy grace
'Doth the eye of earth still witness how vainglory is thy way.

'If I saw thee meek and lowly, pale of visage and demure,
'Then my love for thee would deepen and my yearning win the day;

'Then if aught I saw of blemish in thy frame, O lover mine,
'I would perfect and complete it by mine own bright beauty's ray.'

Whosoever sees his failings in the mirror of his heart
And doth make his nature perfect, all the realms of soul doth sway.

O Khayali, shouldst thou meet with woe, a childlike heart's the balm;
If thou seekest to be mighty, be thou lowly, lowly aye.'
